author: Gluck
title: Orpheus calls Eurydice
where: *Orfeo ed Euridice*, Act 3, Scene 1, with Act 1, Scenes 1 and 2
about: Orpheus, a singer, has gone down among the dead to bring back his wife, Eurydice. The god Love set the terms: he must not look at her until they are out of the underworld, and must not tell her why. On the way up she begs for one look; he turns, she dies a second time, and he sings this aria. The second passage sets Love’s terms beside his words before and after the aria; the third is his song at her tomb in Act 1.

lenses.label: Count
lenses.meterName: the line of eight: an accent on the third syllable and on the seventh; a line may stop on the seventh

points.say: Two vowels meet between these words and count as one syllable. Both are still said. The Italian name for this is *sinalefe*.
The line stops on its stressed seventh syllable. It is still a line of eight: an Italian line takes its name from the place of its last accent.
The name is four syllables, stressed on the third: half a line of eight. Its last vowel counts as one with the cry that follows, across the stop. The fifth line begins the same way.

lenses.why: Calzabigi writes the aria in the line of eight, since Petrarch’s time a line of religious verse and of verse for music, and its two fixed stresses hold through the cries and stops of the third line.
lenses.caption: Italian verse counts syllables, and a vowel that ends a word runs into a vowel that begins the next, as after senza. Counted so, all seven lines stress the third syllable and the seventh. Four go on to an eighth and three stop on the seventh. This is the ottonario, the line of eight, since Petrarch’s time a line of religious verse and of verse for music. The speech before the aria is recitative, sung speech: lines of eleven syllables and one of seven, unrhymed until its close. The third line here is three cries with stops between them and still counts eight.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage: each line counted and its stresses marked. The rule of the count, the running together of vowels and the history of the line of eight: Treccani, *Enciclopedia dell’Italiano*, under *versificazione* and *sinalefe*, and the *Vocabolario Treccani* under *ottonario* and *tronco*. The recitative before the aria: the libretto of 1879, p. 20; part of it is in the second passage. What recitative is: Treccani under *recitativo*.

lenses.label: Endings
lenses.why: Each group of the aria ends on a word cut short, a mark of the canzonetta; rhyme comes only in the last four lines, and the two lines that return are alike inside the line.
lenses.caption: Three lines stop on a word cut short: ben for bene, fedel for fedele, Ciel for cielo. A word cut on a consonant at the end of a line is a mark of the canzonetta, a poem in short lines, usually set to music. Each cut ends a group: the two opening lines, the order to answer, the last three lines. Italian arias are as a rule strictly rhymed; here only the last four lines rhyme: fedel, faithful, with Ciel, heaven, and two lines in anza between them. The two opening lines, which return after the seventh, rhyme with nothing. They are alike inside the line: a verb ending in a stressed rò, I shall, then senza, without.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. The cut words and their place in the canzonetta: the *Vocabolario Treccani* under *troncamento* and *canzonetta*, and the *Enciclopedia dell’Italiano* under *rima*. That arias are strictly rhymed: the same encyclopedia under *melodramma, lingua del*. The meanings: the *Vocabolario* under *fedele*, *cielo*, *senza* and *futuro*. The three groups are also the sections of the score.

lenses.label: Calls
lenses.name: apostrophe
lenses.plain: a turning away: the speaker turns from the hearers to speak to someone or something else; here, from speaking about her to speaking to her
lenses.why: The aria turns from speaking about her to speaking to her after she has died, and gives back the order she gave him in this scene, to answer, with the opposite of the name she called him.
lenses.caption: The first two lines speak about her: what to do without Euridice, where to go without his ben, his good, the one he loves. The third turns to her, though she has just died: it calls the name and orders Rispondi, answer. Rhetoric names this turn apostrophe. Earlier in the scene she gave him that order and called him infido, faithless, and both times his reply was to tell her to come and be silent. Now the order is his, and the fourth line says the opposite of her charge: he is her fedel, her faithful one, and pure, truly, even so, insists on it.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. Apostrophe as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines it. What the scene says before the aria, her death, her charge and her order to answer: Act 3, Scene 1 of the libretto of 1879, pp. 17 to 20. The meanings of *ben*, *rispondere*, *infido*, *fedele* and *pure*, and the form of the command: the *Vocabolario Treccani*.

lenses.label: Rondo
lenses.what: the aria as the score sets it: the two opening lines three times, and what comes between
lenses.why: Gluck makes the two opening lines the returning idea of a rondo, in C major at one tempo, so the order and the despair each give way to them; he wrote that its effect hangs on exact pace and expression.
lenses.caption: The score has the two opening lines three times, each time in C major and at the first tempo. Together they take about half its 70 bars. Between them come the order to answer and the last three lines; each slows to Adagio, stops on a pause and gives way to the same two lines. An idea that keeps returning makes a rondo. The libretto prints the two lines twice, so the middle return is the score’s. Gluck wrote in 1770 that the least change of pace or expression makes this aria a tune for puppets, and a contemporary is reported to have said that the melody would suit words of the opposite sense.
lenses.stands: The form, key and tempo marks: Gluck’s *Orpheus* in Alfred Dörffel’s full score (Peters), pp. 132 to 135, bars counted for this page; the libretto of 1879, p. 20. Rondo: the *Vocabolario Treccani*. Gluck’s remark: the dedication of *Paride ed Elena* (1770), as Ernest Newman gives it in English, *Gluck and the Opera*, p. 93. The contemporary is Boyé, as Eduard Hanslick reports him, *Vom Musikalisch-Schönen*, chapter 2.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: What he must not tell her is the ban itself, named in the line before.
Love called the terms a *pact* and a *ban*. *Law* is Orpheus’s word for them, here and in three other places of the libretto.
The word comes again in the sixth line of the aria.
The fifth line of the aria has the same verb. The dictionary’s first example of this sense is a line of Petrarch.

lenses.why: Two words of the recitative, left and help, return in the aria’s last lines; serious opera before the Romantics drew its language from the line of Petrarch, Tasso and Metastasio.
lenses.caption: Love has forbidden Orpheus to look at Eurydice before they leave the underworld. Here Love adds that he must not tell her, and names the price: he loses her and lives on wretched. In Act 3 Orpheus says that he calls her in vain, has no soccorso, help, and is left no consiglio, counsel. The aria’s last lines take up the words for help and for what is left, and hope replaces counsel. Serious opera before the Romantics drew its language from the line of Petrarch, Tasso and Metastasio.
lenses.stands: The meanings: the *Vocabolario Treccani*, under each word. What Love forbids before these lines: the libretto of 1879, Act 1, Scene 2. The words that return are in the first passage. The line of Petrarch, the dictionary’s first example under *avanzare*, is line 32 of number 268 of his *Canzoniere*. The language of serious opera: the *Enciclopedia dell’Italiano* under *melodramma, lingua del*.

lenses.label: Return

ties.say: Love says it of him: *you lose her*. He says it of himself: *I lose her*. The verb is the same and one letter of it has changed. Each time it ends the line.
Six words come back in the same order, and as before they begin the next line: *and again, and forever*.
After the aria the last three of the six come a third time. Now the wish is his own: *let the pain end, and forever*.
Love said that he would live on. He wants the pain to end with his life.

lenses.why: Calzabigi has Orpheus tell the loss in the words of Love’s threat, six in the same order, so the threat of Act 1 returns as the fact of Act 3; forever comes a third time when he chooses death.
lenses.caption: Love’s terms are in Act 1; Orpheus’s cry is in Act 3, when Eurydice has died. He puts his loss in Love’s words. Perdi, you lose, becomes perdo, I lose, and the next line begins with the same six words, and again, and forever. A threat in Act 1 is a fact in Act 3, word for word, and the same line goes on to name the legge, the law, and death. After the aria per sempre, forever, comes a third time, now in a wish of his own: that pain may end with life. Love had said he would live on, wretched.
lenses.stands: The marks on the two passages, which stand in Act 1, Scene 2 and in Act 3, Scene 1 of the libretto of 1879. A count of the Italian words for *forever* in that libretto: three times in the dialogue, once more in the prose argument. The meanings: the *Vocabolario Treccani* under *perdere*, *sempre*, *legge*, *vivere* and *finire*.

lenses.label: Measure
lenses.meterName: lines of eleven syllables and of seven: the last accent on the tenth or the sixth; an eleven has another on its fourth or sixth; the other stresses are free

1.0.voice: x x /~ x x /~ ~ x xx/x

p:0.1.voice: x x /~ x x /~ x /~ x /x

lenses.caption: Recitative is sung speech, and its verse is looser than an aria’s: lines of eleven syllables and some of seven, mostly without rhyme. Love’s four lines count eleven, eleven, seven, eleven, and one sentence runs through them, over three line ends. Orpheus’s three whole lines before the aria are elevens too; inside they break into short cries, and the vowels still run together across the stops. Of the lines shown whole only two rhyme, the last two of Love’s speech, desìo with addio: the rhyme closes the speech, and Love’s aria follows. Orpheus’s speech also ends on a rhymed pair, just before his aria.
lenses.why: Calzabigi writes both speeches in the loose verse of recitative, elevens and sevens without rhyme, and marks the end of a speech with one rhymed pair; the eleven holds Love’s long sentence and Orpheus’s broken cries alike.
lenses.stands: The marks on the two passages: each whole line counted. What recitative is, and how its verse differs from an aria’s: Treccani, under *recitativo*, and the *Enciclopedia dell’Italiano* under *melodramma, lingua del*, *versificazione* and *sinalefe*. That Love’s aria follows these lines, and that Orpheus’s speech ends on a rhymed pair before his: the libretto of 1879, pp. 9, 10 and 20.

points.say: Three vowels meet here, across the semicolon, and count as one syllable.
A line of seven among the elevens. The sentence runs on through it.
The speech ends on a rhyme with the line before, the only rhyme in it. Love’s aria follows.
Three cries in a row. The vowels run together across the first two exclamation marks, and the line still counts eleven.

pair.label: Orpheus, Act 3, before and after the aria

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.why: The strophe pairs the stopped rhymes that mark the canzonetta and keeps one rhyme waiting; Calzabigi puts the word answers where that rhyme closes, in all three strophes, and the first says that she does not answer.
lenses.caption: Each half of the strophe, a stanza of the song, is two lines that rhyme at once and a third that waits: così with dì, then asconde; dolor with cor, then risponde, which rhymes with asconde three lines later. The four lines that rhyme at once stop on their last accent, and dolor and cor are words cut short, dolore and core: such rhymes are a mark of the canzonetta, a poem in short lines, usually set to music. The strophe’s one long reach of rhyme ends on risponde, answers. The sentence it closes says that she does not. The next two strophes end on the same word and the same rhyme.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. What rhyme is, and that stopped rhymes mark the canzonetta: Treccani, *Enciclopedia dell’Italiano*, under *rima*, and the *Vocabolario Treccani* under *canzonetta* and *troncamento*. The other two strophes: the libretto of 1879, p. 8. The meaning of *risponde*: the *Vocabolario* under *rispondere*.

lenses.label: Strophes
lenses.what: the three strophes of the song, and what answers in each

strophes.setting: when day shows itself and when it hides
strophes.says: the idol of his heart does not answer him

strophes.setting: on the shore where she died
whether the sun gilds the day or goes into the waves
strophes.says: a brook, pitying his tears, answers him

every strophe.how the sevens count: by the place of the last accent: a line that stops on its stressed sixth syllable is still a seven, and four lines of the strophe shown do
every strophe.rhyme: a a b c c b
every strophe.first line: the same but for its verb

between.recitative: he calls her name twice and asks her shade where she is
he calls her name twice; the woods have learned it from him
he turns on the gods of the underworld and resolves to seek her there

lenses.why: Calzabigi ends all three strophes on the same word, answers, and in none of them does Eurydice answer; the verb returns twice in Act 3, last in the aria, where Orpheus orders her to.
lenses.caption: The song has three strophes built alike, with recitative between. Each begins with the same line but for its verb: Chiamo, I call; then Cerco, I seek; then Piango, I weep. Each ends on risponde, answers, and on the same rhyme. The first says that she does not answer him. In the second Echo alone answers, in the third a brook. In the aria of Act 3 he orders her to answer, by name, and that is the last time the libretto uses the verb.
lenses.stands: The three strophes as the libretto of 1879 prints them, p. 8; the first is the passage shown. A count of the verb *rispondere* in that libretto: five times, the aria’s the last. The meanings of *chiamare*, *cercare*, *piangere* and *rispondere*: the *Vocabolario Treccani*. How a line of verse is counted: the *Enciclopedia dell’Italiano* under *versificazione*.

lenses.label: English

ties.say: Calzabigi’s line is about her: *I call my good*, the one I love. The English line is said to her.
*Dì* is day: *when the day shows itself*. The English names the *sun*.
*Hides* becomes *fall*, which rhymes with the first English line. The Italian rhymes its first two lines.
*Grief* becomes *sighs*, the English rhyme word, with a second adjective before it.
The Italian says that she does not answer him. The English leaves him out and says *never*.

lenses.why: Maggioni makes short English lines that rhyme in a pattern of his own, and the rhymes move the sense twice. His first line addresses her, as the Italian printed with it does; Calzabigi’s strophes speak about her.
lenses.caption: The English is Manfredo Maggioni’s, from a libretto in both languages published for the Metropolitan Opera House. He keeps the short lines and in each half rhymes the first with the third: call with fall, sighs with replies. The rhymes move the sense in two places: asconde, hides, becomes fall, and dolor, grief, becomes sighs. His first line says thee, and so does the Italian printed with it in that libretto, a reworked text in four acts. Calzabigi’s line is about her, his ben, his good. In the three strophes Orpheus does not address her; he does that in the recitative between them, and in the aria of Act 3.
lenses.stands: The marks on the two versions. The English is [Maggioni’s](#/read/orpheus/act-1:17), from the libretto in Italian and English that F. Rullman of New York published for the Metropolitan Opera House; the Italian printed beside it there was read in a scan of that book. The meanings of the Italian words: the *Vocabolario Treccani*. Whom Orpheus addresses in the rest of the song: the libretto of 1879, p. 8.

auden.says: No account of this opera by Auden has been found. The one place found where he names it is an essay of 1948 on the Greeks, and there it marks a date. He grants that, for sustained creative work in a single medium, the seventy-five years or so of Athenian drama are surpassed by the 125 years from Gluck’s *Orpheus* to Verdi’s *Otello*, which he calls “the golden age of European opera.” *Orpheus* stands first among the nine opera libretti on his list for the course.
auden.source: “The Greeks and Us” (1948), in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), p. 8

sources: The text: Ranieri de’ Calzabigi, *Orfeo ed Euridice*, the libretto of Gluck’s opera (first performed in Vienna in 1762), in the Italian of the libretto that Ricordi printed in Milan for a performance at the Conservatory in the spring of 1879, compared with the libretto printed in Bologna in 1771 (Stamperia del Sassi). The English set beside it is from [the Italian and English libretto](#/read/orpheus) in four acts that F. Rullman of New York published for the Metropolitan Opera House, which names Manfredo Maggioni as editor and translator.

The score: Christoph Willibald Gluck, *Orpheus: Oper in drei Akten*, full score edited by Alfred Dörffel (Leipzig: C. F. Peters, undated; the editor’s foreword says he was given the work in 1866), no. 43, pp. 132–135, and that foreword.

Treccani, *Enciclopedia dell’Italiano* (2011): *versificazione* and *rima* (Claudio Ciociola), *sinalefe* (Sergio Bozzola and Luciano Romito), *melodramma, lingua del* (Fabio Rossi). Treccani, *Enciclopedia on line*: *recitativo*.

*Vocabolario Treccani* (treccani.it/vocabolario). For the verse: *ottonario*, *tronco*, *troncamento*, *canzonetta*, *rondò*, *futuro*, *imperativo*. For the words: *abbandono*, *ascondere*, *avanzare*, *bene*, *cercare*, *chiamare*, *cielo*, *consiglio*, *cuore*, *desio*, *dì*, *divieto*, *dolore*, *dovere*, *fedele*, *fiero*, *finire*, *infido*, *invano*, *legge*, *nuovo*, *patto*, *perdere*, *piangere*, *pure*, *rispondere*, *rivelare*, *sempre*, *senza*, *soccorso*, *sventurato*, *vita*, *vivere*.
Eduard Hanslick, *Vom Musikalisch-Schönen* (Leipzig: Rudolph Weigel, 1854; the example was added in the second edition, 1858, p. 25), chapter 2: what Boyé said of the aria, as Hanslick reports it.
Ernest Newman, *Gluck and the Opera* (London: Bertram Dobell, 1895), pp. 93–94 and 145: Gluck’s dedication of *Paride ed Elena* (1770) in English, and the key of the aria.
Petrarch, *Canzoniere*, no. 268, line 32, in *Le rime*, edited by Giuseppe Salvo Cozzo (Florence: Sansoni, 1904), p. 259.
W. H. Auden, “The Greeks and Us” (1948), in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), p. 8.
The reading list for English 135, University of Michigan, 1941, as reproduced by Alan Jacobs, “Auden’s Syllabus” (blog.ayjay.org, October 1, 2012): the opera libretti.
caveats: The Italian is Calzabigi’s libretto as Ricordi printed it in Milan in 1879, read by machine and checked against the printed pages and against a libretto printed in Bologna in 1771. No libretto or score printed in Vienna was seen.

That print has a wrong letter in the aria’s first line, which is shown here as the print gives it where the two opening lines return. The print sets the aria as four lines and three; the space after the second line is not the print’s.

The English is Manfredo Maggioni’s, from a libretto published for the Metropolitan Opera House, where it faces a reworked Italian text in four acts and the aria stands in Act 4; it does not always give Calzabigi’s sense.

The stresses marked are one reader’s hearing, and a few light stresses could fairly be marked otherwise; the counts follow the rule that vowels meeting between words count as one syllable, also across a stop.

The aria’s form and its seventy bars are those of Dörffel’s score for Peters, which follows the Paris version of 1774 with Orpheus’s part put back in its first range; this page was made without hearing the record on it. Boyé’s remark is known through Hanslick, Gluck’s through Newman’s English.
